en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Familiarity from the Section of Puzzling Questions (Meṇḍakapañha)
6. The Question Concerning the Elephant King Chaddanta and Jotipāla “Venerable Nāgasena, this was indeed said by the Blessed One concerning the elephant king Chaddanta:
‘While he was grasping [the lotus stalk], thinking, “I shall kill him,”’”
He saw the saffron robe, the banner of the seers;
touched by suffering, this perception arose:
‘The banner of the Arahants is beyond reproach by the virtuous.’”
And yet it is said:

“When he was the young brahmin Jotipāla, he reviled and abused the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with the words ‘shaveling’ and ‘wretched ascetic,’ using harsh and unseemly speech.
If, venerable Nāgasena, the Bodhisatta, while still an animal, honored the saffron robe, then...
Indeed, that statement that "the Blessed One Kassapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was reviled and abused with disparaging words,
with the term 'shaveling' and the term 'ascetic,' and with harsh, unseemly speech by the young brahmin Jotipāla" is false.
If [it were true] that the Blessed One Kassapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, [was so treated] by the young brahmin Jotipāla with the term 'shaveling' and the term 'ascetic'...
If he has been reviled and abused with unseemly and harsh words, then that statement— that "the Kāsāva robe was honored by the elephant king Chaddanta"—
is likewise false. If it was by an animal-born Bodhisatta, while experiencing a sensation that was hard, rough, and bitter, [and] by a hunter...
The saffron robe is honored; why, being a human being with mature knowledge and mature enlightenment,
would you not honor it upon seeing the Blessed One Kassapa— the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one endowed with the ten powers, the Leader of the World, the most exalted,
blazing with dark radiance, the most excellent and supreme, clad in the finest and most beautiful Kāsī saffron robes?
"This too is a dilemma with two sides that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
"This was indeed spoken, Great King, by the Blessed One concerning the elephant king Chaddanta: 'He might kill me... [and so on] ...he is not one to be reviled.'"

And the young Brahmin Jotipāla reviled and insulted the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with the words "shaveling" and "wretched ascetic," using harsh and unseemly speech on account of his birth and his lineage.
Great King, the young Brahmin Jotipāla was born into a family that lacked faith and confidence;
his parents, sisters, brothers, female and male slaves, servants, and attendants were devotees of Brahmā and held Brahmā in high esteem, for they believed: "Only the Brahmins are supreme."
‘Pavara’ means they revile and loathe the rest of those who have gone forth;
having heard their words, the young brahmin Jotipāla, being invited by Ghaṭīkāra the potter to see the Teacher, spoke thus:
‘But what is the point of seeing that shaven-headed ascetic?’
Just as, Great King, ambrosia becomes bitter when mixed with poison, and just as cold water becomes hot when it encounters fire;
even so, Great King, the young brahmin Jotipāla was born into a family lacking faith and confidence. Having become blind by virtue of his birth, he reviled and abused the Tathāgata.

Just as, Great King, a great mass of blazing, fiercely burning fire, though radiant, becomes cool and black—its splendor and heat destroyed—when it encounters water, resembling a fully ripened nigguṇḍī fruit; [so it was with him].
In just this way, Great King, the young brahmin Jotipāla—meritorious, faithful, and possessing the vast radiance of wisdom—was born into a family that was faithless and lacking in confidence.
Because of his birth into such a family, he became as if blind; yet, having reviled and insulted the Tathāgata, he approached him and, recognizing the qualities of the Buddha, became like a servant.
Having gone forth in the teaching of the Conqueror, he attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
“...and having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the formless attainments (*samāpatti*), he went to the Brahma-world.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This is the sixth dilemma concerning Jotipāla, starting from the time of the elephant’s tusks.
